Proteus is important, especially in the context of staghorn calculi and xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis, but it is not the most common agent.
Pseudomonas is an opportunistic pathogen often associated with hospital-acquired UTIs, but is far less common than E. coli.
E. coli is the predominant uropathogen due to its presence in the intestinal tract and specific adhesins like P-fimbriae.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 927 (Book Page): More than 85% of urinary tract infections are caused by the gram-negative bacilli that are normal inhabitants of the intestinal tract. By far the most common is Escherichia coli.

category: Define acute and chronic cystitis
statement: In the pathological progression of chronic cystitis, 'cystitis cystica' is morphologically defined by which of the following?
options: The presence of foamy macrophages with PAS-positive inclusions
Retraction of von Brunn nests to produce cystic spaces lined by flattened urothelium
Gas-filled vesicles within the muscularis propria
Fibrous tissue encasing the retroperitoneal segment of the ureter
Massive infiltration of the lamina propria by mast cells
correctOption: Retraction of von Brunn nests to produce cystic spaces lined by flattened urothelium
optionExplanations: Foamy macrophages with PAS-positive inclusions (Michaelis-Gutmann bodies) define malakoplakia.
Cystitis cystica occurs when the downward-growing nests of urothelium (von Brunn nests) develop central cystic spaces, often as a response to chronic irritation.
Gas-filled vesicles are the hallmark of emphysematous cystitis, not cystitis cystica.
Fibrous tissue encasing retroperitoneal structures describes sclerosing retroperitoneal fibrosis, an extrinsic cause of ureteral obstruction.
Mast cell infiltration is a feature of interstitial cystitis, whereas cystitis cystica is a metaplastic/proliferative change.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 955 (Book Page): epithelial cells in the center of the nest undergo metaplasia and take on a cuboidal or columnar appearance (cystitis glandularis) or retract to produce cystic spaces lined by flattened urothelium (cystitis cystica).

category: Define pyelonephritis and enumerate its types
statement: A 24-year-old pregnant woman presents with sudden onset of high-grade fever, chills, and severe pain at the right costovertebral angle. Urinalysis reveals numerous neutrophils and leukocyte casts. What is the most likely diagnosis, and what is the significance of the casts?
options: Chronic Pyelonephritis; the casts signify long-term scarring
Acute Glomerulonephritis; the casts indicate glomerular capillary leakage
Cystitis; the casts indicate severe bladder wall irritation
Urolithiasis; the casts represent mineralized matrix around stones
Acute Pyelonephritis; the casts confirm renal involvement
correctOption: Acute Pyelonephritis; the casts confirm renal involvement
optionExplanations: Chronic pyelonephritis is usually more insidious or involves recurrent episodes; a sudden systemic febrile presentation in pregnancy is typical of the acute form.
Acute glomerulonephritis presents with red blood cell casts and nephritic features (hypertension, edema), not systemic suppurative symptoms and pus casts.
Cystitis (lower UTI) does not present with leukocyte casts, as casts are only formed within the renal tubules, not the bladder.
Urolithiasis typically presents with hematuria and renal colic but not leukocyte casts unless there is a secondary infection like pyelonephritis.
The clinical triad of fever, flank pain, and pus (leukocyte) casts is pathognomonic for acute pyelonephritis, with the casts localizing the infection to the kidney parenchyma.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 929 (Book Page): Acute pyelonephritis usually presents with a sudden onset of pain at the costovertebral angle and systemic evidence of infection... The finding of leukocyte casts, typically rich in neutrophils (pus casts), indicates renal involvement, because casts are formed only in tubules.

category: Define acute and chronic cystitis
statement: Which of the following factors best explains why females exhibit a significantly higher incidence of bacterial cystitis compared to males in the absence of instrumentation?
options: The anatomic proximity of the shorter female urethra to the rectum facilitating coliform colonization
The absence of vesicoureteral reflux in the female population during micturition
The presence of antibacterial properties in vaginal secretions compared to prostatic fluid
Increased bladder capacity in females leading to higher volumes of residual urine stasis
Hormonal changes that specifically inhibit the adherence of P-fimbriated Escherichia coli
correctOption: The anatomic proximity of the shorter female urethra to the rectum facilitating coliform colonization
optionExplanations: The shorter length of the female urethra drastically reduces the distance coliform bacteria from the fecal reservoir must travel to reach the bladder, making ascending infection far more likely.
Vesicoureteral reflux is a mechanism that carries infection from the bladder to the kidneys; it does not explain the initial higher incidence of bladder-localized cystitis in females.

Vaginal secretions do not typically contain the same potent antibacterial properties found in prostatic fluid; the lack of prostatic fluid in females is a risk factor, not the presence of vaginal secretions.
Bladder capacity is not the primary anatomical difference cited for infection rates; rather, it is the urethral length and the absence of protective prostatic secretions.
Hormonal changes in females are actually noted to affect bacterial adherence in ways that can increase susceptibility, rather than providing a protective inhibition of coliforms.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 925 (Book Page): In the absence of instrumentation, urinary infections are much more common in females, and this has been ascribed to the shorter urethra in females, the absence of antibacterial properties in prostatic fluid, hormonal changes affecting bacterial adherence to the mucosa, and urethral trauma during sexual intercourse.

category: Identify the causes, morphological aspect & outcome of hydronephrosis
statement: Even in the presence of complete urinary tract obstruction, glomerular filtration persists for a significant period. What physiological mechanism allows for this continued filtration?
options: Ureteral peristalsis generating negative pressure in the Bowman space
Diffusion of the filtrate back into the renal interstitium and perirenal spaces
Dilation of the efferent arteriole to reduce intraglomerular hydrostatic pressure
Active transport of metabolic waste by the tubular epithelial cells into the renal vein
Shunting of blood flow from the cortex to the medulla via the vasa recta
correctOption: Diffusion of the filtrate back into the renal interstitium and perirenal spaces
optionExplanations: Ureteral peristalsis is generally inhibited or ineffective in the face of high distal pressure and does not create a vacuum in the Bowman space sufficient to overcome the back-pressure of obstruction.

Glomerular filtration can continue despite obstruction because the generated filtrate leaks into the interstitium and perirenal spaces, eventually entering the lymphatics and veins, which prevents the hydrostatic pressure in the Bowman space from immediate equalization with capillary pressure.

Dilation of the efferent arteriole would actually decrease GFR by lowering the glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure. In hydronephrosis, GFR is maintained by the escape of fluid, not by arteriole dilation.

Tubular cells are primarily damaged in hydronephrosis, leading to impaired reabsorption and secretion; they do not compensate for obstruction by actively transporting bulk filtrate components into the venous system.

While blood flow is altered, specifically medullary flow is diminished due to compression, shunting does not explain why filtration continues in the presence of a blocked outflow tract for the urine itself.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 943 (Book Page): Even with complete obstruction, glomerular filtration persists for some time because the filtrate subsequently diffuses back into the renal interstitium and perirenal spaces, from where it ultimately returns to the lymphatic and venous systems.

category: Define pyelonephritis and enumerate its types
statement: During the pathogenesis of an ascending urinary tract infection, which bacterial mechanism is most critical for the colonization of the urothelium against the flow of urine?
options: Formation of a thick polysaccharide capsule to resist phagocytosis by neutrophils
Direct invasion of the peritubular capillaries via the hematogenous route
Secretion of urease to alkalinize the urine and promote salt precipitation
Interaction of P-fimbriae adhesins with specific receptors on urothelial cells
Production of Shiga-like toxins that induce apoptosis in the distal tubular epithelium
correctOption: Interaction of P-fimbriae adhesins with specific receptors on urothelial cells
optionExplanations: While capsules aid in evading the host immune system, they do not mediate the specific adherence to the urothelial surface required for ascending infection.
This describes the hematogenous route of infection, which is less common than the ascending route and does not involve urethral colonization steps mentioned in the stem.
Urease production is characteristic of Proteus species and contributes to staghorn calculi but is not the primary mechanism for initial colonization in the distal urethra.
Adhesins located on the P-fimbriae of uropathogenic bacteria (like E. coli) are essential for anchoring the bacteria to the urothelium, preventing them from being washed away by micturition.
Shiga-like toxins are associated with Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS), not the standard ascending pathway of pyelonephritis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 925 (Book Page): which involves adhesive molecules (adhesins) on the P-fimbriae (pili) of bacteria that interact with receptors on the surface of urothelial cells.

category: Describe morphological features of different type of cystitis
statement: A 28-year-old female presents with acute onset of suprapubic pain and frequent urination. A biopsy of the bladder mucosa is performed. Which of the following microscopic findings is the primary morphological hallmark of the acute phase of this patient’s condition?
options: Mononuclear inflammatory cell infiltration
Granular, PAS-positive Michaelis-Gutmann bodies
Broad, bulbous polypoid projections with marked edema
Mucosal hyperemia and neutrophilic infiltrate
Accumulation of lymphoid follicles in the submucosa
correctOption: Mucosal hyperemia and neutrophilic infiltrate
optionExplanations: Mononuclear inflammatory infiltrates are the histological hallmark of chronic cystitis, which results from the persistence of a bacterial infection. Acute cystitis is dominated by polymorphonuclear leukocytes (neutrophils).

Michaelis-Gutmann bodies are specific mineralized concretions within lysosomes of macrophages and are diagnostic of malakoplakia, a specific chronic inflammatory reaction related to phagocyte dysfunction, not acute cystitis.

Broad, bulbous polypoid projections associated with submucosal edema are characteristic of polypoid cystitis, often caused by chronic irritation from instrumentation like catheters, rather than acute primary infection.

According to the reference, the acute phase of cystitis is characterized morphologically by hyperemia of the mucosa (increased blood flow) and an infiltration of neutrophils, which may be associated with an inflammatory exudate.

The presence of lymphoid follicles within the bladder mucosa and underlying wall is characteristic of follicular cystitis, rather than simple acute cystitis. Follicular cystitis is a distinct variant that reflects localized lymphoid aggregation.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 953 (Book Page): In acute cystitis, there is hyperemia of the mucosa and neutrophilic infiltrate, sometimes associated with exudate.

category: Identify the causes, morphological aspect & outcome of hydronephrosis
statement: Following the surgical relief of a complete bilateral urinary tract obstruction, which of the following physiological events is most commonly observed?
options: Rapid onset of secondary hyperparathyroidism and renal osteodystrophy.
Development of essential mixed cryoglobulinemia.
A massive postobstructive diuresis rich in sodium chloride.
Sudden conversion to a nephrotic state with heavy lipiduria.
Persistent oliguria due to irreversible glomerular scarring.
correctOption: A massive postobstructive diuresis rich in sodium chloride.
optionExplanations: This is a chronic complication of long-term end-stage renal disease, not an acute response to the relief of an obstruction.
This is a systemic vascular condition associated with Hepatitis C, unrelated to obstructive uropathy.
Correct. Postobstructive diuresis is a well-known phenomenon where the kidneys excrete massive volumes of water and salt as they recover and clear accumulated urea and fluids.
Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by glomerular basement membrane damage; relieving an obstruction does not cause sudden heavy proteinuria/lipiduria.
If caught in time, the obstruction is reversible, and the kidneys enter a diuresis phase rather than persistent oliguria.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 946 (Book Page): [Curiously, after relief of complete urinary tract obstruction, postobstructive diuresis occurs. This can often be massive, with the kidney excreting large amounts of urine that is rich in sodium chloride.]

category: Discuss the etiology and pathogenesis of different types of stones
statement: Which specific type of renal calculus is most frequently associated with the development of 'staghorn calculi' that create a branching cast of the renal pelvic and calyceal system?
options: Magnesium ammonium phosphate stones
Pure uric acid stones
Pure calcium oxalate stones
Xanthine stones
Cystine stones
correctOption: Magnesium ammonium phosphate stones
optionExplanations: Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) stones are called 'infection stones' because they form rapidly in the presence of alkaline urine caused by urea-splitting bacteria, often growing to fill the entire collecting system.
Uric acid stones are typically smaller and do not exhibit the massive, rapid accretion required to form a staghorn cast of the renal pelvis.
Calcium oxalate stones are usually smaller and localized within the calyces; they rarely form the massive branching structures characteristic of staghorn stones.
Xanthine stones are extremely rare metabolic stones and are not listed as a primary cause of branching staghorn calculi in standard medical pathology texts.
Cystine stones can occasionally grow large, but they are significantly less common than infection-induced stones as a cause of staghorn configurations.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 947 (Book Page): Indeed, so-called staghorn calculi occupying large portions of the renal pelvis are frequently a consequence of infection.

category: Describe morphological features of different type of cystitis
statement: In the pathogenesis of malakoplakia, what is the specific biochemical nature and cellular location of the Michaelis-Gutmann bodies?
options: Eosinophilic proteinaceous droplets within the cytoplasm of umbrella cells.
Crystalline lattices of viral particles within the nuclei of von Brunn nests.
Glycogen-rich inclusions within the nuclei of squamous metaplastic cells.
Laminated mineralized concretions within the lysosomes of large foamy macrophages.
Lipid-filled vacuoles located within the mitochondria of neutrophils.
correctOption: Laminated mineralized concretions within the lysosomes of large foamy macrophages.
optionExplanations: Eosinophilic droplets might be seen in protein reabsorption states in the kidney tubules, but they do not describe the mineralized structures seen in malakoplakia.
Crystalline viral lattices describe polyomavirus (BK/JC) infection morphology, whereas malakoplakia is an antibacterial defect involving macrophage lysosomes.
Glycogenation is common in the trigone of women as a normal variant, but it is unrelated to the chronic inflammatory mineralized bodies of malakoplakia.

Michaelis-Gutmann bodies are pathognomonic laminated mineralized concretions consisting of calcium and iron deposited within enlarged lysosomes of macrophages, resulting from defective phagolysosomal degradation of bacteria.
While foamy macrophages (von Hansemann cells) are present, the Michaelis-Gutmann bodies are mineralized calcium deposits in lysosomes, not lipid vacuoles in mitochondria.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 956 (Book Page): In addition, laminated mineralized concretions resulting from deposition of calcium in enlarged lysosomes, known as Michaelis-Gutmann bodies, are typically present within the macrophages.

category: Identify the causes, morphological aspect & outcome of hydronephrosis
statement: What is the most common cause of hydronephrosis identified in the pediatric population, specifically infants and children?
options: Vesicoureteral reflux
Ureteropelvic junction (UPJ) obstruction
Renal calculi
Meatal stenosis
Posterior urethral valves
correctOption: Ureteropelvic junction (UPJ) obstruction
optionExplanations: Vesicoureteral reflux is the most common 'congenital anomaly' associated with infection, but for the specific diagnosis of hydronephrosis, UPJ obstruction is the lead cause.
UPJ obstruction, often due to abnormal smooth muscle organization or stromal collagen at the junction, is the most common etiology in pediatric hydronephrosis cases.
Renal calculi are much more common in adults (ages 20-30) than in infants/children.
Meatal stenosis is a cause of distal obstruction but is far less common as a cause of upper tract hydronephrosis compared to UPJ obstruction.
Posterior urethral valves are a significant cause of bilateral hydronephrosis in males, but UPJ obstruction is more frequently encountered overall.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 954 (Book Page): Ureteropelvic junction (UPJ) obstruction is the most common cause of hydronephrosis in infants and children.

category: Identify the causes, morphological aspect & outcome of hydronephrosis
statement: Which of the following is the most accurate pathological definition of hydronephrosis?
options: Ischemic necrosis of the renal papillae primarily seen in diabetic patients.
Formation of branching magnesium ammonium phosphate stones within the collecting system.
Dilation of the renal pelvis and calyces associated with progressive kidney atrophy due to urine outflow obstruction.
Acute inflammation of the renal pelvis caused by ascending bacterial infection.
Formation of multiple expanding cysts that destroy renal parenchyma through genetic mutations.
correctOption: Dilation of the renal pelvis and calyces associated with progressive kidney atrophy due to urine outflow obstruction.
optionExplanations: This describes papillary necrosis, a complication that can occur with pyelonephritis or diabetes, but it is not the definition of hydronephrosis itself.
This describes staghorn calculi (urolithiasis), which can cause hydronephrosis, but the stone formation is not the definition of the resulting renal dilation and atrophy.

Hydronephrosis specifically refers to the mechanical dilation of the collecting system and the subsequent pressure-induced atrophy of the renal tissue caused by obstruction at any level of the urinary tract.
This describes acute pyelonephritis, which is a suppurative inflammation rather than a mechanical dilation resulting in parenchymal atrophy.
This describes polycystic kidney disease, which is a hereditary cystic disorder rather than a manifestation of obstructive uropathy.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 945 (Book Page): Hydronephrosis is the term used to describe dilation of the renal pelvis and calyces associated with progressive atrophy of the kidney due to obstruction to the outflow of urine.

category: g asymptomatic proteinuria or hematuria detected during routine testing, nephrotic syndrome, acute nephritic syndrome, and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN)
statement: A 24-year-old male presents to the emergency department with hemoptysis and dark, coca-cola colored urine. Laboratory studies reveal a serum creatinine of 4.5 mg/dL (Baseline 1.0 mg/dL). Immunofluorescence microscopy of a renal biopsy reveals a sharp, continuous linear pattern of IgG staining along the glomerular basement membrane. Which mechanism is primarily responsible for this patient's clinical presentation?
options: T-cell mediated injury leading to widespread podocyte foot process effacement
Deposition of circulating immune complexes containing exogenous antigens
In situ formation of immune complexes against the PLA2R podocyte antigen
Activation of the alternative complement pathway by C3 nephritic factor
Antibodies directed against the NC1 domain of the alpha-3 chain of Type IV collagen
correctOption: Antibodies directed against the NC1 domain of the alpha-3 chain of Type IV collagen
optionExplanations: Widespread podocyte foot process effacement without immune deposits is the hallmark of Minimal Change Disease, which presents as Nephrotic Syndrome.
Circulating immune complexes typically result in a granular immunofluorescence pattern, not the linear pattern described in the scenario.
Antibodies to the PLA2R antigen are associated with Membranous Nephropathy, which presents with a granular immunofluorescence pattern and nephrotic syndrome.
Alternative complement pathway activation by C3 nephritic factor is the mechanism for Dense Deposit Disease (C3 Glomerulopathy), not anti-GBM disease.

The patient has Goodpasture Syndrome (RPGN Type I), where autoantibodies against the NC1 domain of the alpha-3 chain of Type IV collagen cause pulmonary hemorrhage and linear IgG deposition in the kidney.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 909 (Book Page): Anti-GBM antibody–mediated disease, characterized by linear deposits of IgG... The antigen common to the alveoli and GBM is a peptide within the noncollagenous portion of the α3 chain of collagen type IV.

category: Identify the causes, morphological aspect & outcome of hydronephrosis
statement: In advanced cases of chronic hydronephrosis, the kidney can be transformed into a thin-walled cystic structure. What is the typical maximum diameter this structure may achieve according to pathological studies?
options: 15 to 20 cm
30 to 40 cm
10 to 12 cm
5 to 7 cm
2 to 3 cm
correctOption: 15 to 20 cm
optionExplanations: Terminal hydronephrosis can lead to massive expansion of the pelvis, essentially destroying the kidney and leaving a fluid-filled sac of this size.
This exceeds the typical reported pathological sizes for hydronephrotic kidneys.
While large, the reference specifies an even larger potential for expansion.
This represents a slightly enlarged kidney but not the massive expansion seen in terminal hydronephrosis.
This is too small; 2-3 mm is the size of some small pelvic stones, while 2-3 cm would be a minor cyst.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 944 (Book Page): In far-advanced cases, the kidney may become transformed into a thin-walled cystic structure having a diameter of up to 15 to 20 cm.

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic pyelonephritis
statement: In a histological section of a contracted kidney, several dilated tubules are observed to be lined by flattened epithelium and filled with glassy, pink-staining casts. Which term is used to describe this specific morphological feature of chronic pyelonephritis?
options: Thyroidization
Hyalinosis
Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions
Endocapillary proliferation
Fibrinoid necrosis
correctOption: Thyroidization
optionExplanations: Thyroidization occurs in chronic pyelonephritis when atrophic tubules dilate and fill with proteinaceous casts, superficially resembling the follicles of the thyroid gland.
Hyalinosis refers to the accumulation of eosinophilic, homogeneous material (plasma proteins) in glomerular structures, not the specific colloid-like filling of tubules.
Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions are nodular glomerulosclerosis found specifically in diabetic nephropathy, not the tubular changes associated with chronic pyelonephritis.
Endocapillary proliferation involves an increase in cells within the glomerular capillary loops, typical of acute proliferative glomerulonephritis, not chronic tubular changes.
Fibrinoid necrosis is a feature of malignant hypertension or vasculitis involving blood vessel walls, characterized by the deposition of fibrin and cell death.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 931 (Book Page): Dilated tubules with flattened epithelium may be filled with casts resembling thyroid colloid (thyroidization).

category: Define pyelonephritis and enumerate its types
statement: What is the critical pathophysiological mechanism that allows bacteria to bypass the one-way valvular function of the ureteral insertion during an ascending infection?
options: Seeding of the renal cortex via the peritubular capillary network
Hyper-filtration of the glomerular basement membrane inducing retrograde pressure
Obliteration of the P-fimbriae adhesins on the bacterial cell wall
Loss of the antibacterial properties of prostatic fluid in females
Congenital shortening of the intravesical portion of the ureter
correctOption: Congenital shortening of the intravesical portion of the ureter
optionExplanations: Seeding via capillaries refers to the hematogenous route of infection, which is far less common than the ascending route facilitated by reflux.
Glomerular filtration is a downstream process and does not influence the mechanical integrity of the vesicoureteral junction.
P-fimbriae are essential for bacterial colonization; their obliteration would actually prevent infection rather than facilitate reflux into the kidneys.
The absence of antibacterial prostatic fluid explains the higher incidence of UTIs in females but is not the mechanical mechanism for the failure of the ureteral valve.

Vesicoureteral reflux occurs when the normal flap-valve mechanism of the ureter is compromised, usually due to an abnormally short intravesical ureteral segment that fails to compress under bladder pressure.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 926 (Book Page): Reflux is most often due to a congenital absence or shortening of the intravesical portion of the ureter, such that the ureter is not compressed during micturition.

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic pyelonephritis
statement: A patient with long-standing chronic pyelonephritis and significant polar scarring begins to develop proteinuria in the nephrotic range (>3.5g/day). Which pathological change in the preserved glomeruli best explains this progression?
options: Formation of epithelial crescents within the Bowman space.
Linear deposition of anti-GBM antibodies along the capillary loops.
Secondary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis due to adaptive hypertrophy.
Infiltration of the glomerular tuft by polymorphonuclear neutrophils.
Diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement membrane by immune complexes.
correctOption: Secondary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis due to adaptive hypertrophy.
optionExplanations: Crescent formation is seen in Rapidly Progressive Glomerulonephritis (RPGN), which causes acute renal failure rather than the slow progression of chronic pyelonephritis to secondary sclerosis.
Linear antibody deposition is pathognomonic for Goodpasture Syndrome/Anti-GBM disease, not the secondary sclerosing changes of chronic renal parenchymal disease.

When significant renal mass is lost due to chronic pyelonephritic scarring, the remaining glomeruli undergo adaptive hypertrophy and hemodynamic changes, leading to secondary FSGS and nephrotic-range proteinuria.
Neutrophilic infiltration of the glomerulus is a feature of acute inflammatory conditions like post-streptococcal GN, not the chronic scarring stage of pyelonephritis.
Diffuse thickening by immune complexes describes Membranous Nephropathy, which is a primary glomerular disease, not a secondary consequence of pyelonephritic scarring.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 931 (Book Page): Individuals with chronic pyelonephritis and reflux nephropathy who develop proteinuria in advanced stages show secondary FSGS... attributable to the adaptive glomerular alterations secondary to loss of renal mass.

category: Define various presentations of glomerulonephritis e
coreConcept: Differential diagnosis of major glomerular syndromes
statement: Which of the following clinical features most reliably distinguishes a nephritic presentation from a nephrotic presentation during an initial workup?
options: A persistent decline in the glomerular filtration rate (GFR).
Grossly visible or microscopic hematuria with dysmorphic red cell casts.
Elevation of blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine.
The presence of lipiduria and oval fat bodies in the urine.
The presence of pitting periorbital edema.
correctOption: Grossly visible or microscopic hematuria with dysmorphic red cell casts.
optionExplanations: Both syndromes can result in a decreased GFR, so this parameter alone does not distinguish the underlying presentation type.

Hematuria, particularly with dysmorphic cells and casts, signifies active glomerular inflammation (nephritis), whereas nephrotic syndrome is primarily a disorder of the filtration barrier without significant inflammation.
Azotemia (elevated BUN/Creatinine) can occur in both, though it is a more 'classic' early feature of the inflammatory nephritic process.
Lipiduria and oval fat bodies are characteristic of the hyperlipidemic state found in nephrotic syndrome, not nephritic syndrome.
Edema is present in both syndromes, though it is usually much more severe and generalized in nephrotic syndrome.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 896 (Book Page): Nephritic syndrome is a clinical entity caused by inflammatory glomerular disease and is dominated by the acute onset of either grossly visible hematuria (red blood cells in urine) or microscopic hematuria with dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts on urinalysis...

category: Describe morphological features of different type of cystitis
statement: In the condition known as cystitis cystica et glandularis, the morphological transformation involves the retraction of which anatomical structures to produce cystic spaces lined by metaplastic epithelium?
options: von Brunn nests
Michaelis-Gutmann bodies
Hunner ulcers
Fibroepithelial polyps
Michaelis-Gutmann bodies
correctOption: von Brunn nests
optionExplanations: Option C is correct. von Brunn nests are downward-growing clusters of urothelium that can hollow out (cystica) or undergo glandular metaplasia (glandularis).
Option A is incorrect as Michaelis-Gutmann bodies are calcified intracellular inclusions in macrophages, not urothelial structures.
Option D refers to the chronic mucosal ulcers found in the classic late phase of interstitial cystitis.
Option E refers to benign mesenchymal tumors found in the ureter or bladder, not a metaplastic inflammatory process.
Option B is a repetition and is incorrect as it refers to malakoplakia.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 955 (Book Page): These are common lesions of the urinary bladder in which nests of urothelium (von Brunn nests) grow downward into the lamina propria. Here, epithelial cells... retract to produce cystic spaces lined by flattened urothelium (cystitis cystica).

category: Discuss the etiology and pathogenesis of different types of stones
coreConcept: Uric Acid Nephrolithiasis in Hematological Malignancies
statement: A 52-year-old male with Chronic Myeloid Leukemia undergoes aggressive chemotherapy. Following treatment, he develops acute, severe flank pain and hematuria. Urinalysis reveals a persistent urinary pH of 5.2. A plain abdominal radiograph shows no visible stones. What is the most likely etiology of his stone formation?
options: Urea-splitting bacterial infection
Hyperoxaluria due to enteric disease
Idiopathic hypercalciuria
Excessive cell turnover leading to hyperuricosuria
Genetic defect in amino acid reabsorption
correctOption: Excessive cell turnover leading to hyperuricosuria
optionExplanations: Infection with urea-splitting bacteria would cause alkaline urine (high pH), whereas this patient has a low urinary pH (5.2).
Hyperoxaluria leads to calcium oxalate stones, which are radiopaque and usually visible on X-ray.
Idiopathic hypercalciuria would likely result in radiopaque calcium stones, which were not seen on the X-ray.

Leukemias involve rapid cell turnover, which is exacerbated by chemotherapy (tumor lysis). This releases massive amounts of purines, metabolized to uric acid. In acidic urine (pH 5.2), uric acid precipitates into radiolucent stones.
A genetic defect in amino acid reabsorption refers to cystinuria, which is not typically associated with leukemia or tumor lysis syndrome.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 947 (Book Page): Uric acid stones are common in individuals with hyperuricemia, such as patients with gout, and diseases involving rapid cell turnover, such as the leukemias... it is thought that a tendency to excrete urine of pH below 5.5 may predispose to uric acid stones, because uric acid is insoluble in acidic urine. In contrast to the radiopaque calcium stones, uric acid stones are radiolucent.

category: Describe morphological features of different type of cystitis
statement: A 55-year-old female presents with severe, intermittent suprapubic pain and dysuria for 8 weeks. Cystoscopy reveals punctate hemorrhages known as 'glomerulations' and mucosal fissures. What is the histological relationship between this condition and bladder carcinoma?
options: It is a direct precursor to squamous cell carcinoma
It involves the same FGFR3 mutations as papillary urothelial carcinoma
It is characterized by Michaelis-Gutmann bodies that mimic low-grade tumors
Its primary role in biopsy is to exclude carcinoma in situ (CIS)
It often exhibits intestinal metaplasia preceding adenocarcinoma
correctOption: Its primary role in biopsy is to exclude carcinoma in situ (CIS)
optionExplanations: Chronic squamous metaplasia, often due to Schistosomiasis or chronic irritation, is the precursor to squamous cell carcinoma, not interstitial cystitis.

FGFR3 mutations are hallmarks of non-invasive papillary urothelial neoplasms, whereas interstitial cystitis is an inflammatory condition without documented shared oncogenic mutations with papillary tumors.
Michaelis-Gutmann bodies are part of malakoplakia and are not mentioned in the context of interstitial cystitis morphology or its differential with cancer.
Interstitial cystitis (defined by glomerulations and pain) clinically mimics CIS. Therefore, the textbook emphasizes that a biopsy is primarily used to ensure the patient does not actually have CIS.
Intestinal metaplasia is associated with cystitis glandularis (intestinal variant) and is a precursor to adenocarcinoma, which is not the pathology described here.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 954 (Book Page): The main role of biopsy is to rule out carcinoma in situ (CIS), which clinically mimics interstitial cystitis.

category: Define acute and chronic cystitis
statement: A patient is diagnosed with emphysematous cystitis. Which of the following pathophysiological mechanisms characteristically defines this specific variant of bladder inflammation?
options: Epithelial replacement by keratinizing squamous cells due to chronic irritation.
Chronic mucosal ulceration leading to transmural fibrosis and bladder contraction.
Systemic viral reactivation of the BK polyomavirus in the bladder wall.
Focal failure in the development of the normal detrusor musculature.
Production of gas-filled vesicles within the bladder wall by specific bacteria.
correctOption: Production of gas-filled vesicles within the bladder wall by specific bacteria.
optionExplanations: Squamous metaplasia is a protective transformation of the urothelium in response to chronic injury, such as schistosomiasis, rather than an acute gas-forming infection.
Chronic mucosal ulceration and transmural fibrosis are characteristic of the late, ulcerative phase of interstitial cystitis, often involving Hunner ulcers.
BK virus is associated with hemorrhagic cystitis, particularly in immunocompromised or transplant patients, rather than gas production.
Focal failure of the detrusor musculature is the underlying mechanism for congenital diverticula, not the infectious process of emphysematous cystitis.
Emphysematous cystitis is caused by gas-forming organisms like Clostridium perfringens or certain E. coli strains, which produce gas as a metabolic byproduct within the bladder tissues.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 953 (Book Page): Gas-forming bacteria (such as Clostridium perfringens) result in emphysematous cystitis (gas-filled vesicles in the bladder wall).

category: Define acute and chronic cystitis
statement: Which specific condition must be clinically excluded when a patient presents with symptoms mimicking interstitial cystitis, such as severe suprapubic pain and dysuria, to ensure an accurate diagnosis?
options: Vesicoureteral reflux
Emphysematous cystitis
Acute pyelonephritis
Carcinoma in situ (CIS)
Malakoplakia
correctOption: Carcinoma in situ (CIS)
optionExplanations: Vesicoureteral reflux is an anatomical abnormality leading to pyelonephritis, not a symptomatic pain syndrome that mimics interstitial cystitis.
Emphysematous cystitis is an acute bacterial infection with gas in the bladder wall, easily distinguished by imaging and clinical severity.
Acute pyelonephritis presents with fever and CVA tenderness, which distinguishes it from the chronic pain of interstitial cystitis.
Carcinoma in situ can present with the same irritative voiding symptoms and pain as interstitial cystitis; therefore, a biopsy is often required to rule out malignancy.
Malakoplakia presents with yellow mucosal plaques and is histologically distinct, not a primary clinical mimic that requires exclusion via pain syndrome criteria.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 954 (Book Page): The main role of biopsy is to rule out carcinoma in situ (CIS), which clinically mimics interstitial cystitis.

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic pyelonephritis
coreConcept: Macroscopic Differentiation of Chronic Renal Diseases
statement: A pathologist is examining an 'end-stage' kidney and notes that the scarring is asymmetric and irregular, with coarse corticomedullary scars overlying blunted, deformed calyces. This morphological pattern is most distinctive for differentiating which condition from chronic glomerulonephritis?
options: Chronic pyelonephritis
Acute tubular injury
Malignant nephrosclerosis
Lupus nephritis
Analgesic nephropathy
correctOption: Chronic pyelonephritis
optionExplanations: Chronic pyelonephritis and reflux nephropathy are unique in causing pelvocalyceal damage (blunting/deforming), whereas glomerulonephritis causes symmetric, fine scarring.
Acute tubular injury primarily shows tubular epithelial swelling or necrosis rather than permanent, coarse cortical scarring and calyceal deformity.
Malignant nephrosclerosis typically presents with petechial hemorrhages and 'flea-bitten' kidneys, not coarse corticomedullary scars and calyceal blunting.
Lupus nephritis involves diverse glomerular inflammatory patterns and, when chronic, leads to more uniform scarring without the specific calyceal blunting of pyelonephritis.
While analgesic nephropathy also affects calyces, the specific combination of asymmetric coarse scars and blunted calyces is the classic hallmark of chronic pyelonephritis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 930 (Book Page): The hallmarks of chronic pyelonephritis are coarse, discrete, corticomedullary scars overlying dilated, blunted, or deformed calyces, and flattening of the papillae.

category: Define pyelonephritis and enumerate its types
coreConcept: Pathological Contrast of Chronic Renal Diseases
statement: Which macroscopic finding is most useful in distinguishing chronic pyelonephritis from chronic glomerulonephritis during a post-mortem renal evaluation?
options: Fine, even granularity of the cortical surface resembling grain leather.
Irregular, asymmetric corticomedullary scars overlying blunted calyces.
Diffuse and symmetrical scarring of both kidneys.
Presence of multiple small, translucent cortical simple cysts.
Generalized, uniform thinning of the renal cortex without pelvic involvement.
correctOption: Irregular, asymmetric corticomedullary scars overlying blunted calyces.
optionExplanations: A fine, leather-like granularity is the classic macroscopic description of nephrosclerosis associated with benign hypertension.
The involvement of the pelvocalyceal system (blunted calyces) and irregular polar scarring are diagnostic hallmarks unique to chronic pyelonephritis/reflux nephropathy.
Diffuse and symmetrical scarring is characteristic of chronic glomerulonephritis, whereas chronic pyelonephritis is typically asymmetric and irregular.
Simple cysts are common post-mortem findings without clinical significance and do not characterize the chronic inflammatory scarring of pyelonephritis.
Chronic pyelonephritis must involve the calyces and pelvis; uniform thinning without such involvement suggests other chronic kidney diseases.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 930 (Book Page): The hallmarks of chronic pyelonephritis are coarse, discrete, corticomedullary scars overlying dilated, blunted, or deformed calyces, and flattening of the papillae.

category: Define pyelonephritis and enumerate its types
statement: Which of the following best provides the clinical-pathological definition of pyelonephritis?
options: Sterile inflammation of the renal interstitium caused by hypersensitivity to drugs.
Inflammation affecting the tubules, interstitium, and renal pelvis.
Infection limited to the mucosal lining of the urinary bladder and distal urethra.
An autoimmune-mediated injury targeting the glomerular basement membrane.
Ischemic necrosis of the renal papillae due to analgesic abuse or diabetes.
correctOption: Inflammation affecting the tubules, interstitium, and renal pelvis.
optionExplanations: This describes drug-induced tubulointerstitial nephritis, which lacks the characteristic involvement of the renal pelvis seen in pyelonephritis.
Pyelonephritis is defined by its involvement of the renal pelvis along with the functional units (tubules) and the supporting connective tissue (interstitium).
This describes cystitis and urethritis, which are lower urinary tract infections and do not involve the renal parenchyma or pelvis as required for pyelonephritis.
This describes glomerulonephritis, specifically anti-GBM disease, which is distinct from the infectious and inflammatory process of pyelonephritis.
This defines papillary necrosis, which is a complication of pyelonephritis in specific contexts like diabetes, but is not the general definition of pyelonephritis itself.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 925 (Book Page): Pyelonephritis is one of the most common diseases of the kidney and is defined as inflammation affecting the tubules, interstitium, and renal pelvis.

category: g asymptomatic proteinuria or hematuria detected during routine testing, nephrotic syndrome, acute nephritic syndrome, and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN)
statement: A 26-year-old male presents with sudden onset of hemoptysis and rapidly declining renal function. Laboratory studies show high titers of anti-GBM antibodies. A renal biopsy reveals extensive crescent formation in 85% of the glomeruli. Which of the following describes the most likely target of the pathogenic antibodies in this patient?
options: The streptococcal pyogenic exotoxin B (SpeB) planted in the subendothelial space.
The cytoplasmic granule protein proteinase-3 (PR3) in neutrophils.
The P-fimbriae adhesins of nephritogenic Escherichia coli.
A peptide within the noncollagenous portion of the alpha-3 chain of collagen type IV.
The M-type phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R) on the basal surface of podocytes.
correctOption: A peptide within the noncollagenous portion of the alpha-3 chain of collagen type IV.
optionExplanations: SpeB is the major antigen implicated in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN), which usually causes Type II (Immune Complex) RPGN if it progresses, rather than the anti-GBM pattern described.

PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA) is associated with Type III (Pauci-immune) RPGN, such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis. This type lacks the linear IgG deposits characteristic of the anti-GBM antibodies seen in this patient.
P-fimbriae are involved in the pathogenesis of ascending pyelonephritis by facilitating bacterial adherence to urothelium, not in the autoimmune crescentic glomerulonephritis of Goodpasture syndrome.

Goodpasture syndrome (Type I RPGN) is caused by autoantibodies against the noncollagenous (NC1) domain of the alpha-3 chain of Type IV collagen. Because this chain is present in both glomerular and pulmonary alveolar basement membranes, patients present with both renal failure and hemoptysis.

PLA2R is the target antigen in primary membranous nephropathy, which typically presents as nephrotic syndrome rather than a rapidly progressive crescentic nephritic syndrome with pulmonary hemorrhage.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 909 (Book Page): The antigen common to the alveoli and GBM is a peptide within the noncollagenous portion of the alpha 3 chain of collagen type IV.

category: Discuss the etiology and pathogenesis of different types of stones
statement: A patient is found to have a large 'staghorn' calculus occupying the renal pelvis. Pathological analysis identifies the presence of urea-splitting bacteria. What is the primary pathophysiological mechanism leading to the formation of this specific stone type?
options: Hyperabsorption of calcium from the intestine due to vitamin D excess
Increased urinary excretion of uric acid leading to nucleation
Loss of urinary inhibitors like nephrocalcin and pyrophosphate
Genetic defect in the renal tubular reabsorption of dibasic amino acids
Conversion of urea to ammonia resulting in an alkaline urinary pH
correctOption: Conversion of urea to ammonia resulting in an alkaline urinary pH
optionExplanations: Hyperabsorption of calcium leads to hypercalciuria and calcium oxalate stones, but does not drive the formation of magnesium ammonium phosphate salts.
Increased uric acid leads to uric acid stones or provides a seed for calcium oxalate, but does not characterize the magnesium-based staghorn calculi associated with infection.
While a deficiency in inhibitors like nephrocalcin can enhance stone formation generally, it is not the specific driving mechanism for struvite stone precipitation triggered by bacteria.
Genetic defects in amino acid reabsorption describe the pathogenesis of cystine stones, which are not typically the primary cause of infection-related staghorn calculi.
Bacteria such as Proteus produce urease, which hydrolyzes urea into ammonia, raising the urinary pH. This alkaline environment is essential for the precipitation of magnesium ammonium phosphate.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 947 (Book Page): Magnesium ammonium phosphate stones are formed largely after infections by urea-splitting bacteria (e.g., Proteus and some staphylococci) that convert urea to ammonia. The resultant alkaline urine causes the precipitation of magnesium ammonium phosphate salts.

category: Define acute and chronic cystitis
statement: Which microorganism is identified as the most frequent etiologic agent responsible for the development of acute cystitis?
options: Candida albicans
Klebsiella pneumoniae
Schistosoma haematobium
Escherichia coli
Proteus mirabilis
correctOption: Escherichia coli
optionExplanations: Candida albicans causes cystitis primarily in specific populations like the immunosuppressed or those on long-term antibiotics, not the general population.
Klebsiella is a common coliform cause but is less frequent than E. coli.
Schistosoma haematobium is an important cause in specific endemic regions (Middle East/Africa) but is not the most common cause globally or in general practice.
Correct. The text explicitly identifies E. coli as the most common etiologic agent of cystitis among the coliforms.
Proteus is a common coliform cause but is listed as following E. coli in frequency.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 953 (Book Page): [The most common etiologic agents of cystitis are the coliforms: Escherichia coli, followed by Proteus, Klebsiella, and Enterobacter.]

category: Define acute and chronic cystitis
coreConcept: Stasis as a predisposing factor for cystitis
statement: Chronic cystitis is frequently a secondary complication of underlying conditions that promote urinary stasis. Which of the following is a classic cause of urinary outflow obstruction that predisposes to chronic bacterial cystitis in older males?
options: Vesicouterine fistulae.
Congenital shortening of the intravesical ureter.
Primary amyloidosis of the ureter.
Benign prostatic hyperplasia.
Primary exophytic urothelial papilloma.
correctOption: Benign prostatic hyperplasia.
optionExplanations: Vesicouterine fistulae involve an abnormal connection between the bladder and uterus, occurring in females, often as a result of surgery or trauma.

Congenital shortening of the intravesical ureter is the mechanism for vesicoureteral reflux, which primarily leads to pyelonephritis rather than being the classic cause of bladder outlet obstruction and stasis.
Amyloidosis of the ureter is a rare cause of ureteral obstruction, not the classic bladder outlet obstruction associated with the clinical presentation of chronic cystitis.

Benign prostatic hyperplasia (prostatic hypertrophy) causes narrowing of the urethra, leading to incomplete bladder emptying (stasis), which allows bacteria to multiply and cause chronic or recurrent cystitis.
While bladder neoplasms can cause obstruction, a primary papilloma is rare and typically small, whereas prostatic hyperplasia is an extremely common cause in the older male population.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 956 (Book Page): Cystitis is sometimes a secondary complication of an underlying disorder associated with urinary stasis, such as prostatic hypertrophy, cystocele, calculi, or bladder neoplasms.

category: Identify the causes, morphological aspect & outcome of hydronephrosis
statement: A 4-year-old boy presents with a history of urinary frequency, a weak stream, and a large midline suprapubic mass. Imaging reveals a massively distended bladder and bilateral hydroureter with thinned renal parenchyma. If this condition is left untreated, which morphological transformation is most characteristic of the final, far-advanced stage of his renal disease?
options: Shrunken, granular kidneys with focal corticomedullary scars overlying blunted calyces
Kidneys with large, yellowish-orange nodules that may be confused with renal cell carcinoma
Transformation of the kidney into a thin-walled cystic structure with total obliteration of the pyramids
Small, contracted kidneys with a reduced number of renal lobes and pyramids (six or fewer)
Enlarged kidneys containing numerous expanding cysts that destroy the intervening parenchyma
correctOption: Transformation of the kidney into a thin-walled cystic structure with total obliteration of the pyramids
optionExplanations: This describes chronic pyelonephritis with reflux nephropathy, characterized by asymmetric scarring and pelvocalyceal damage.
This describes xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis, a rare form of chronic inflammation associated with Proteus infections, not simple obstructive uropathy.
In end-stage hydronephrosis, the sustained high pressure leads to extreme parenchymal thinning and loss of internal structures like the renal pyramids.
This describes true renal hypoplasia, which is a congenital failure of development rather than an acquired obstructive atrophy.
This is the classic description of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, where cysts arise from the tubules themselves, not from a dilated pelvis.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 944 (Book Page): In far-advanced cases, the kidney may become transformed into a thin-walled cystic structure having a diameter of up to 15 to 20 cm with striking parenchymal atrophy, total obliteration of the pyramids, and thinning of the cortex.

category: Define various presentations of glomerulonephritis e
coreConcept: Genetics of Thin Basement Membrane Nephropathy
statement: Thin basement membrane nephropathy, also known as benign familial hematuria, is most frequently caused by mutations in genes encoding which of the following proteins?
options: Alpha-actinin 4
Podocin
Nephrin
Heparan sulfate proteoglycan
Alpha-3 or Alpha-4 chains of Type IV collagen
correctOption: Alpha-3 or Alpha-4 chains of Type IV collagen
optionExplanations: Alpha-actinin 4 mutations are linked to autosomal dominant forms of FSGS.
Podocin mutations (NPHS2) are associated with steroid-resistant FSGS.
Nephrin mutations are associated with the Finnish type of congenital nephrotic syndrome, not thin basement membrane disease.
Loss of heparan sulfate is a biochemical change in many glomerular diseases but is not the primary genetic cause of this hereditary thinning.
Thin basement membrane disease is part of the spectrum of Type IV collagen disorders (along with Alport syndrome), specifically involving the alpha-3 and alpha-4 chains.
citation: In book "Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease", Page 922 (Book Page): The anomaly in thin basement membrane nephropathy has also been traced to mutations in genes encoding alpha 3 or alpha 4 chains of type IV collagen.

category: Describe morphological features of different type of cystitis
statement: Which of the following morphological hallmarks is diagnostic of malakoplakia upon microscopic examination of the urinary bladder mucosa?
options: Laminated mineralized concretions within macrophages
Lymphoid follicles with germinal centers
Keratinizing squamous epithelium with dysplasia

correctOption: Laminated mineralized concretions within macrophages
optionExplanations: Michaelis-Gutmann bodies are the pathognomonic feature of malakoplakia; they are laminated, calcified inclusions within foamy macrophages (von Hansemann cells) resulting from incomplete bacterial digestion.
Lymphoid follicles with germinal centers are characteristic of follicular cystitis, which is typically a chronic inflammatory response, not malakoplakia.
Keratinizing squamous epithelium is a metaplastic change seen in chronic irritation or Schistosoma infection, which may progress to squamous cell carcinoma, distinct from malakoplakia.
Nests of urothelium growing downward into the lamina propria are known as von Brunn nests, which can lead to cystitis cystica or glandularis.
Broad bulbous projections associated with marked submucosal edema define polypoid cystitis, often a result of catheter-induced irritation.
